piano-5.subject: piano
piano-5.title: Keep the bass steady while the melody moves
piano-5.context: Use the four-beat example: left C3 holds while the right plays E4–D4–C4–D4. We will separate the two hand jobs before joining them.

steps.title: Find the bass key
steps.prompt: Which key does the left hand begin on? Use a note name such as C3.
steps.reasoning: C3 is the C one octave below middle C. Its 3 names the register. The right hand begins on E4 at the same moment.
stuck: I mix up the numbers
C3 and C4 are two pitches an octave apart. Finger 3 is your middle finger; that is a different use of the number. Here, C3 tells you where the low key is.
I cannot find low C
Find middle C, C4, then move to the next C on its left: C3. Each C is immediately left of a group of two black keys.

mistakes.C4: C4 is middle C, where the right thumb is prepared. Move one octave left to C3 for this bass part.

steps.title: Count the left-hand presses
steps.prompt: Over the complete four beats, how many times does the left hand press C3?
steps.reasoning: Press C3 once on beat 1 and keep the key down through 2, 3 and 4. Release at the next 1. Holding a note is not a new press on each beat.
stuck: I keep copying the right hand

Try just two counts on a table. On 1 touch one left fingertip and your right middle finger down together. On 2, keep the left fingertip touching while you swap the right middle finger for the index finger.
I do not know when to release
Say 1–2–3–4–1 evenly. Press on the first 1 and release on the second 1. The last counted 4 still gets its full beat.

mistakes.4: Four presses would restart the bass on every beat. This accompaniment has one bass attack underneath four right-hand attacks.
mistakes.0: The left hand does begin the note on beat 1. It then holds without pressing again.

steps.title: Move only the right hand
steps.prompt: On beat 2, the left C3 is still down. Which new note does the right hand play?
steps.reasoning: The right begins on E4, then moves one white key left to D4 on beat 2. Its index finger can play D4 while the left hand keeps C3 down.
stuck: I do not know the right-hand route
Prepare thumb over C4, index over D4 and middle over E4. Play middle–index–thumb–index: E4–D4–C4–D4.
Both hands lift together
Practise only the change from beat 1 to beat 2. Keep left C3 down while right E4 releases and right D4 begins. Stop and relax after D4; the whole bar can wait.

mistakes.E4: E4 is the first right-hand note, on beat 1. On beat 2 it releases and D4 begins.
mistakes.C4: C4 arrives on beat 3. First move from E4 to D4 on beat 2.

noun-phrases.subject: spanish
noun-phrases.title: Build an order the other person can use
noun-phrases.context: Use pequeño for small and begin with the item group itself. You may add Quiero before it and por favor after it. This coach checks these specific phrase patterns; it does not judge every possible Spanish sentence.

steps.title: One small coffee
steps.prompt: Write the item group for “a small coffee”.
steps.reasoning: Learn el café as a pair. For an unspecified coffee, use un. Add pequeño after café: un café pequeño.
stuck: I do not know un or una
Café uses masculine agreement: el café, un café. Mesa uses feminine agreement: la mesa, una mesa. Learn each article with its noun.
I do not know the word order
In this model, the size follows the thing: un + café + pequeño. Put quiero in front to make the request.

mistakes.una: Café takes un here, not una: un café pequeño.
mistakes.pequeña: Use pequeño to agree with café in this phrase: un café pequeño.

steps.title: Two small coffees
steps.prompt: Now change only the item group to “two small coffees”.
steps.reasoning: Replace un with dos. Make café and pequeño plural: cafés pequeños. The finished group is dos cafés pequeños.
stuck: What changes for two?
Make three edits: un → dos; café → cafés; pequeño → pequeños. Quiero can stay exactly as it was.
Why does pequeños need s?
It describes the plural noun cafés, so it also becomes plural. The s matches the coffees; it does not mean that you ordered several sizes.

mistakes.café: Dos needs the plural cafés. Add s to café, keeping the written accent.
mistakes.pequeño: The coffees are plural, so the description must be plural too: pequeños.
mistakes.una: Use dos for the quantity. You do not put un or una before dos in this group.

steps.title: Use a different noun
steps.prompt: Write “two small tables”, using mesa for table.
steps.reasoning: Mesa is feminine, so the description uses pequeña. Two makes both words plural: dos mesas pequeñas.
stuck: Which ending belongs to mesa?
Begin with una mesa pequeña. The a in pequeña agrees with mesa in this example. For two, keep the a and add s: pequeñas.
Do all adjectives change like this?
No. Grande stays grande for one coffee or one table, then becomes grandes in the plural. This step deliberately uses pequeño/pequeña so you can follow this particular agreement.

mistakes.pequeños: Pequeños is masculine here; mesa needs pequeñas.
mistakes.pequeño: Use the feminine plural pequeñas with mesas.

count-exchanges.subject: chess
count-exchanges.title: Count both turns before judging the capture
count-exchanges.context: Use the second worked position: White Kg1 and Rd1; Black Kg8, Nd5 and Pe6. Follow Rxd5, then …exd5. Values are rough: knight 3, rook 5. All answers are from White’s viewpoint.

steps.title: What White gains
steps.prompt: After Rxd5, what rough value has White captured?
steps.reasoning: The rook on d1 captures the knight on d5. The knight is worth roughly 3. That is the gain from the first turn, not the final exchange result.
stuck: What does Rxd5 mean?
R means rook, x means captures, and d5 is the destination. The d-file is clear from d1 to d5, so the rook can take the knight.
Which piece should I count?
Count the piece removed: Black’s knight. The white rook moved but is still on the board after this first turn.

mistakes.5: Five is the value of the rook doing the capturing. White has captured the knight, worth about 3.

steps.title: What White gives up
steps.prompt: Black replies …exd5. What rough value does White lose? Enter the positive value of the lost piece.
steps.reasoning: The pawn on e6 captures diagonally onto d5 and removes the white rook. That rook is worth roughly 5. The black pawn stays on d5.
stuck: How can the pawn take the rook?
Black pawns capture diagonally toward lower ranks. From e6 this pawn can capture a white piece on d5. The move is legal in this position.
Do I count the pawn too?
The pawn is the capturer, not another captured piece. After …exd5 the pawn remains on d5. The white rook is the piece removed.

mistakes.3: Three is the knight White gained. On Black’s reply, the piece White loses is its rook, worth about 5.
mistakes.1: One is the pawn’s rough value. The pawn remains on the board; it has taken the rook.

steps.title: Combine gain and loss
steps.prompt: What is White’s change from the complete exchange: gain minus loss? Use a minus sign if White loses value.
steps.reasoning: White gains a knight worth 3 and loses a rook worth 5: 3 − 5 = −2. This describes the exchange change, not an evaluation of every feature of the final position.
stuck: I get the sign backwards
Choose White’s viewpoint and keep it. Black pieces removed are gains; white pieces removed are losses. Three gained minus five lost leaves White two units worse off.
Does −2 prove the move is always bad?
Material is one consideration. A forced mate could justify a sacrifice. This worked position supplies no such benefit; its purpose is to show why you must include the legal recapture.

mistakes.2: The size of the difference is 2, but White gave up more than it gained. From White’s viewpoint the change is −2.
mistakes.3: That counts only White’s capture. Include the rook lost on Black’s reply: 3 − 5.
mistakes.0: The first bishop-for-knight line is roughly level. This line gives up a rook worth 5 for a knight worth 3.
mistakes.8: Adding the two values counts how much was removed in total. The change for White is the gain minus the loss, 3 − 5.

product-rule.subject: calculus
product-rule.title: Account for each strip of new area
product-rule.context: At t=2 s the rectangle is L=3 m by W=4 m. Its length grows at 1 m/s; its width grows at 4 m/s. Find its instantaneous area rate, one strip at a time.

steps.title: The growing length
steps.prompt: What area rate comes from the length growing at 1 m/s along the current 4 m width? Give the number in m²/s.
steps.reasoning: Pair the length rate with the current width: 1 m/s × 4 m = 4 m²/s. A narrow lengthwise extension stretches across the entire old width.
stuck: Why multiply by the width?
If the length grows by a small amount, the new strip runs along all 4 metres of the current width. A 0.01 m length increase would add a 0.01 by 4 strip.
Am I multiplying the two rates?
Use one rate and one size. The current width is 4 m; its rate is separately 4 m/s. They happen to share the number 4 here, but the units show which quantity you used.

mistakes.1: One metre per second is the side’s rate. Multiply by the 4 m width to get a rate of area.
mistakes.12: Twelve is the current area, 3×4, in square metres. This question asks how fast one strip adds area, in square metres per second.

steps.title: The growing width
steps.prompt: What area rate comes from the width growing at 4 m/s along the current 3 m length? Give the number in m²/s.
steps.reasoning: Pair the width rate with the current length: 4 m/s × 3 m = 12 m²/s. This is the second strip, along the other edge.
stuck: Which 3 do I use?
The length is currently 3 m. The growing width adds a strip running along that whole length, so multiply the width rate by 3 m.
Where did the first strip go?
Keep its 4 m²/s aside. This step calculates the other strip only. We will add the two contributions in the next step.

mistakes.4: Four is the first strip’s area rate. For the second strip use the width rate, 4 m/s, multiplied by the current length, 3 m.

steps.title: Both edges together
steps.prompt: Add the two contributions. What is the instantaneous area rate at t=2 s, in m²/s?
steps.reasoning: A′=L′W+LW′=4+12=16 m²/s. The small corner contributes no extra term in the limit. Expanding A=t³+t² gives A′=3t²+2t, also 16 at t=2.
stuck: Why add rather than multiply?
Each term already measures an area rate. Both strips are being added to the same rectangle, so add their rates: 4 m²/s + 12 m²/s.
What about the little corner?
Over a short time h, the corner area is of order h². Dividing the total area change by h leaves a corner contribution of order h, which tends to zero. The two long strips survive that limit.

mistakes.4: Four accounts for just the first strip here. Include the second contribution, 12. If you multiplied the two side rates, check units: m²/s² is not an area rate.
mistakes.12: Twelve accounts for just the second strip. Add the first contribution of 4 m²/s too.
mistakes.16.71: That is the average over h=0.1 s in the figure. The question asks for the instantaneous rate at the starting moment; smaller intervals approach 16.

physics-2.subject: physics
physics-2.title: Turn an energy account into a speed
physics-2.context: Use the second example: a 2 kg sled starts still, drops 5 m, and transfers 36 J to thermal energy. Use g=10 m/s². We will find the energy available, then the energy left for motion, then the speed.

steps.title: Available energy
steps.prompt: How much gravitational potential energy is lost? Give the number in joules.
steps.reasoning: mgh = 2 kg × 10 m/s² × 5 m = 100 J. The height is the vertical drop. Starting from rest means no initial kinetic energy needs to be added.
stuck: What do m, g and h stand for?
Here m=2 kg, g=10 m/s² and h=5 m. Multiply those three given numbers. The product is an energy in joules.
Why use the drop rather than the slope length?
Near Earth, gravitational energy depends on the change in height. A longer route between the same two heights changes travel distance, but not this mgh difference.

mistakes.50: That is g×h, which is energy per unit mass here. Include the 2 kg mass: 2×10×5 = 100 J.
mistakes.64: Sixty-four joules is what remains for motion after the thermal transfer. This first step asks for the full gravitational energy available before that transfer.

steps.title: Energy left as motion
steps.prompt: After the stated 36 J thermal transfer, how much kinetic energy remains? Give the number in joules.
steps.reasoning: The account is 100 J = kinetic energy + 36 J thermal energy. Subtract 36 from 100: kinetic energy is 64 J. The total energy is still accounted for.
stuck: Is energy disappearing?
No. The final account has 64 J kinetic plus 36 J thermal, which totals the original 100 J. Mechanical energy has decreased because some energy is now thermal.
Why not subtract 36 from the speed?
Thirty-six is an energy in joules, not a speed. Subtract it from the 100 J energy account first. Then use the kinetic-energy formula to find speed.

mistakes.100: That would leave all the energy as motion. Include the stated 36 J transfer to thermal energy: 100−36.
mistakes.136: The 36 J is part of the original 100 J account, transferred away from motion. Subtract it to find the kinetic part.
mistakes.36: That is the thermal part. The kinetic part is what remains of the 100 J.

steps.title: From squared speed to speed
steps.prompt: Use ½×2×v²=64. What is the final speed? Give the number in m/s.
steps.reasoning: The half and the mass 2 multiply to 1, leaving v²=64. Take the nonnegative square root: v=8 m/s. Check: ½×2×8² = 64 J, and 64+36 = 100 J.
stuck: I do not know what v² means
v² means v multiplied by itself. We need the nonnegative number whose square is 64. Since 8×8=64, the speed is 8 m/s.
Why did the mass disappear?
For this particular 2 kg sled, the coefficient ½×2 equals 1. We have already used the mass to find the available energy; it was not ignored.

mistakes.64: You have found v². Take the square root to find v: 8×8=64, so the speed is 8 m/s.
mistakes.10: Ten metres per second is the frictionless result. Here 36 J has become thermal energy, leaving only 64 J as motion.
mistakes.32: After ½×2 is simplified, the equation is v²=64. Dividing by 2 again is not needed; take the square root.
mistakes.-8: −8 also squares to 64, but this question asks for speed, a nonnegative magnitude. Use 8 m/s.
